justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift from a baseline level of roughly 58–59 across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 58.3 is anchored heavily to the most recent observed value, with very little expected movement overnight given typical market or index inertia. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 58.5, reflecting a small positive drift assumption consistent with recent momentum. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises to 59.0, incorporating a modest continuation of that trend while acknowledging that mean-reversion forces and changing conditions make any directional bias less reliable over longer periods.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 3 points (56.8–59.8), because overnight moves are historically constrained and regime changes rarely materialize within hours. At one week, the interval expands to 6 points (55.5–61.5), incorporating the possibility of a significant data release, policy announcement, or sentiment shift within that window. At one month, the interval widens to 12 points (53.0–65.0), reflecting the full range of plausible macro developments, seasonal patterns, and cumulative random variation that can accumulate over roughly 20 trading days.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as a surprise central bank decision, an unexpected geopolitical escalation, or a major data print that dramatically revises growth or inflation expectations. On the upside, a strong risk-on rally driven by better-than-expected earnings or a resolution of an ongoing policy uncertainty could push the value well above 65 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a liquidity event, credit scare, or sharp repricing of risk assets could drive the value below 53.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume a relatively stable volatility regime. If realized volatility spikes — as it can during periods of market stress — even the one-day interval could prove too narrow. Structural breaks, such as a sudden change in the underlying index composition or methodology, represent a separate tail risk that probabilistic models built on historical patterns are inherently poorly equipped to capture.
